report.summary: Datalog engines like Soufflé use semi-naive evaluation, B-tree storage, parallel execution, and magic-sets to analyze millions of LOC in minutes (Doop took ~8 min for OpenJDK). CodeQL adds incremental evaluation for commit-snapshot queries. A Datalog layer on a multiplex graph is feasible by exporting relations to Soufflé, but incremental updates remain hard. Short-term: benchmark Soufflé on extracted subgraph relations.
risks: incremental updates may cause latency spikes if full re-evaluation is needed
integration complexity with existing graph db
todos: prototype extraction from multiplex graph to relations
benchmark Soufflé on representative code analysis tasks
assess whether Cypher/GQL recursive features suffice

handoff.suggestion: Integrate Datalog by first treating it as a batch analysis engine: periodically export the relevant portion of the multiplex graph (e.g., call graph, dataflow) as relational facts to Soufflé. Soufflé compiles Datalog rules to C++ and runs in-process; you can embed it as a service. Benchmark against real workloads: Doop reported analyzing OpenJDK (14M LOC) in under 10 minutes with Soufflé; for Daedalus code evolution tasks, the graph is smaller, so inference time may be seconds. If that's acceptable, implement a caching layer that only re-exports changes. For truly interactive latency (<100ms), explore DDlog or write a custom incremental Datalog evaluator that pushes deltas through the rules. Alternatively, check if the multiplex graph DB already supports recursive queries (e.g., Neo4j's Cypher supports variable-length paths) sufficient for your analysis; if yes, Datalog may be overkill. The single most impactful next step: replicate Doop's setup on a sample Java project from your domain, measure Soufflé's latency for your typical analysis, and compute the overhead of graph-to-relations translation.
